lessons.title: arrivederci — "goodbye," i.e. "until we meet again"
lessons.gloss: goodbye (literally "until we see each other again")

segments.text: You can open a conversation in Italian and ask how someone is. Now, close it. The standard goodbye is arrivederci — and, like its French and German cousins, it doesn't say "goodbye" at all. It says "until we see each other again."
arrivederci = ar-ree-veh-DER-chee: a tapped double r, and the final -ci is soft (chee, Italian c before i). Stress the -der-.
Break it into four pieces you can almost read straight off:
a = "to / until" (Latin ad).
ri- = "again" (Latin re- — as in English re-do, re-view).
vedere = "to see" (Latin vidēre becomes English video, vision, evident, provide).
-ci = "us / each other."
Glued: a-(ri)-vedere-ci becomes "to our seeing-one-another-again." You don't say farewell; you promise the next meeting.
The whole family says the same thing.
This "until re-seeing" idea is shared right across the languages you're learning — a lovely thing to notice:

utterances: language: Italian. goodbye: arrivederci. literally: "to our re-seeing".
language: French. goodbye: au revoir. literally: "to the re-seeing" (re + voir, see).
language: German. goodbye: auf Wiedersehen. literally: "on again-seeing" (wieder + sehen).

segments.text: Three languages, one gesture: part by pointing at the reunion, not the parting. (Italian keeps a heavier, final "to God" goodbye too — addio, a Dio — the exact twin of Spanish adiós; but for everyday partings it's arrivederci.)

segments.text: What does arrivederci literally promise? ("Until we see each other again.") What French and German goodbyes share that exact idea? (au revoir, auf Wiedersehen.) Which heavier Italian goodbye means "to God," like Spanish adiós? (addio.) Next: "see you tomorrow" — a domani.
The "until re-seeing" pattern gives you a whole family of goodbyes: just name when. First: a domani, "to tomorrow."
a domani = ah doh-MAH-nee: clean open vowels, stress the -ma-.
a = "to / until" (the same a from arrivederci).
domani = "tomorrow," from Latin dē māne, "from the morning."
That word māne ("morning") is quietly shared across the Romance family, and you may have already met its Spanish child:
Italian domani ("tomorrow") from dē māne.
Spanish mañana from (hōra) māneāna — which means both "morning" and "tomorrow," because tomorrow is "the coming morning."
So a domani literally says "until the morning [to come]." You part by pointing at daybreak.

segments.instruction: Italian domani and Spanish mañana — both from māne, "morning"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: Italian *domani* and Spanish *mañana* — both from *māne*, "morning"]

segments.text: What does domani come from, and what does it literally mean? (Dē māne — "from the morning.") Which Spanish word shares that māne root? (Mañana — morning and tomorrow.) Next: "see you soon" — a presto.
Same frame, new "when": a presto, "to soon." And presto is a word English already borrowed whole — from stage magic and music.
a presto = ah PREH-stoh: clean st, crisp open e.
a = "to / until."
presto = "soon, quickly," from Latin praestō, "at hand, ready, present" (prae- "before" + stō/stāre "stand" — literally "standing before you," ready to hand).
English took presto straight from Italian:
in music, presto means "fast."
in stage magic, "presto!" means "quick — and there it is!"
it shares that stō ("stand") root with stare from your how-are-you chapter, and with English station, stable, status.
So a presto is "until [it is] soon / at hand" — see you before long.

segments.instruction: "presto" as music ("fast") and magic ("presto!") — same word
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "presto" as music ("fast") and magic ("presto!") — same word]

segments.text: What does presto mean, and where has English borrowed it? ("Soon / quickly" — in music and magic.) What "stand" root does it share with stare? (Latin stō/stāre.) Next: "see you later" — a più tardi.
The last "when" in the set: a più tardi, "to later" — literally "to more late." Two small words, both alive in English.
piu-glide — più = pyoo, one gliding syllable (the accent marks the stress).
a più tardi = ah pyoo TAR-dee, tapped r.
a = "to / until."
più = "more," from Latin plūs — the very word English took for plus, and the root of plural, surplus.
tardi = "late," from Latin tardus, "slow, late" becomes English tardy, re-tard ("to slow down"), tardy slip.
Together, più tardi = "more late" = "later." So a più tardi is "until [it's] more-late" — see you later on. (Italian builds "later" as more late, just as English does with the comparative -er.)

segments.text: What do più and tardi mean, and their English cousins? (Più = "more" plus; tardi = "late" tardy.) So a più tardi literally says? ("To more-late" becomes see you later.) Next: put the farewells together.

lessons.title: Practice — saying goodbye in Italian
lessons.gloss: closing a conversation — the full set of Italian goodbyes

segments.text: No new words. You can now open a conversation, ask how someone is, and close it. Run the goodbyes until the right one comes automatically.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the closings

segments.text: Neutral / polite (anyone):
— È stato un piacere. Arrivederci! — Arrivederci!
With a "when" — pick the promise that fits:
— A domani! (see you tomorrow) — A presto! (see you soon) — A più tardi! (see you later — same day).
Casual (a friend): the ciao you learned in Chapter 1 doubles as "bye" —.
— Ciao, a presto!
arrivederci — goodbye ("until we re-see each other"; the au revoir / auf Wiedersehen family). Heavier, final variant: addio ("to God," twin of adiós).
a domani — see you tomorrow (domani from dē māne, "morning"; kin of Spanish mañana).
a presto — see you soon (presto from praestō, "at hand" — the English music/magic word).
a più tardi — see you later (più plus, tardi tardy).

segments.text: Open and close a whole tiny exchange without stopping.

Which goodbye means "until we see each other again"? (Arrivederci.) Which says "to the morning"? (A domani.) Which Italian goodbye matches Spanish adiós — "to God"? (Addio.) You can now run an Italian conversation start to finish.
